beginner.headline: New Graduates Use AI at Work
beginner.brief: Lotte Underwood has finished university and uses AI tools for much of her work. Her team's AI tools are computer programs that help with tasks like research and making pictures. She checks their work and shares it with other people in her team. She also joins meetings to learn how these tools can help customers. Underwood wants to learn other skills for her job too. Patel builds AI tools that give information to different teams. Patel also looks for tasks that AI could do, such as work that people repeat. Some graduates work with experienced staff to learn their jobs. They move to a different area of work every six months. Claire Reed believes too much AI work may not help graduates build their future careers. She says workers need AI skills and knowledge of what their customers want.

intermediate.headline: AI Graduate Jobs Raise Questions About Workplace Learning
intermediate.brief: Some companies are creating graduate roles focused on artificial intelligence, or AI, even as the technology is linked to graduate job cuts. Recent graduate Lotte Underwood works in public relations, a field concerned with organisations' public image, but mainly uses AI. She manages AI agents, checks their outputs and passes the results to colleagues who work directly with clients and the media. However, she also wants to pick up traditional public relations skills that her current role does not focus on. Dillan Patel began developing an internal chatbot to collect the knowledge of a senior employee who was preparing to retire. He now develops further AI agents and identifies manual or repetitive jobs that the technology could do. Research by PwC suggests that AI allows employers to expect more senior abilities from people in entry-level jobs. Cian Clinton uses around ten AI agents each day and says AI makes him feel more like an equal team member. He believes this experience will help his career progress faster. Simon Pratt says AI knowledge matters, but his company's two-year graduate programme focuses on learning the trade. Graduates on this programme rotate across four areas, spending six months in each and learning alongside experienced managers. Claire Reed warns that graduate roles focused too heavily on AI may not support long-term career progress. She argues that AI skills need to be combined with sector knowledge and an understanding of what clients actually want.

advanced.headline: Graduate AI Roles Raise Questions About Professional Development
advanced.brief: Although AI is seen as a major factor behind graduate job cuts, companies are also establishing graduate positions specifically focused on the technology. Recent graduate Lotte Underwood works in public relations but spends more time using AI than carrying out conventional public relations work. Her remit includes managing AI agents, checking their results and passing material to colleagues who deal directly with clients and the media. The dedicated AI team has built around 30 agents for activities ranging from industry research and interview preparation to helping clients produce clearer briefs. At engineering software company Stride, graduate Dillan Patel was assigned to develop a chatbot designed to capture the knowledge of a senior employee transitioning into retirement. His subsequent role includes identifying manual or repetitive work that AI could perform across the company. Maxwell envisages graduates challenging an organisation to consider AI holistically, examining both potential applications and opportunities for business growth. If AI makes graduate jobs more integral to an organisation, Maxwell argues, employers can build a more loyal and engaged workforce whose members contribute meaningfully earlier. An analysis of 2.4 million US entry-level jobs found that the roles most influenced by AI were seven times more likely to require traditionally senior abilities, including motivational leadership and strategic decision making. PwC found that entry-level roles with higher expectations had grown by 35% since 2019, whereas other entry-level roles had declined by 10%. Clinton says greater opportunities to implement ideas have brought substantially more responsibility. Clinton argues that advancement is becoming less dependent on accumulated knowledge and more dependent on critical thinking and an understanding of processes. Underwood would like to gain traditional public relations experience beyond her current responsibilities, but remains confident about her future in the agency's growing AI team. Pratt describes a programme in which graduates move through four areas at six-month intervals, learning alongside senior relationship managers. Those graduates learn about financial products, prepare credit papers for lenders and develop customer relationships before progressing to managing entire transactions. Claire Reed cautions that graduate roles dominated by AI will not necessarily support long-term career progression. Reed nevertheless regards a baseline of AI literacy as a requirement for every graduate job. Only when AI expertise is coupled with an understanding of what clients actually want can it support a graduate's career, one contributor argues.
